lesson.title: Stem Hunters
lesson.subtitle: Strip -en at speed — the stem is the verb's DNA

hook.title: One Stem, Six People
hook.content: Stop reading German verbs as whole words. Read them as stem + ending. Strip the dictionary -en and what remains — lern-, komm-, trink-, mach-, denk- — is the verb's DNA: it never changes, and every single person is built from it. You learned the endings in the Conjugation Roots lesson; today you drill the dissection until stripping -en becomes instant. Hunters who own the stem never memorize conjugation tables — they assemble them on sight.

footnotes.title: Old English Did the Same
footnotes.content: Old English verbs worked identically: lǣran 'to teach' had the stem lǣr- and wore ic lǣre, þū lǣrest, hē lǣrþ. German never stopped building verbs this way — English just stopped showing the seams.

pattern.title: Dissect, Then Rebuild
pattern.content: Step one — dissect: lernen → lern-, kommen → komm-, trinken → trink-, machen → mach-, denken → denk- (note the nk: the k of think survives intact!). Step two — rebuild the whole row from the stem: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. One stem, six tiles: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. The wir and sie forms wear the full dictionary -en; du wears the Shakespearean -st; er keeps the archaic -th as -t. Nothing else ever happens to a regular verb.
pattern.linguist_note: denken hides a historical wrinkle: du denkst preserves the stem, but the past tense will later surprise you (dachte, not denkte). Regular verbs keep the stem untouched forever; denken is already practicing its escape.

exercises.explanation: Stem 'komm-' + wir's full '-en' = kommen — the dictionary form does double duty as the wir-form.
lern- + the six personal tiles builds every form: lerne, lernst, lernt, lernen...

exercises.prompt: The hunter's ledger — match each infinitive with its stripped stem:
exercises.target_answer: setz-, sitz-, halt-, küss-, zeig-, steh-
exercises.meaning: stems of setzen, sitzen, halten, küssen, zeigen, stehen
exercises.explanation: Six new verbs, one old move: strip the -en and the stem stands naked — setz-, sitz-, halt-, küss-, zeig-, steh- — ready for any of the six endings.

exercises.meaning: ich always takes -e on regular verbs
exercises.explanation: ich wears -e (lerne); lernt belongs to er and ihr. English never says 'I learns' either.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'We want to try things on and go for a stroll'
exercises.meaning: We want to try things on and go for a stroll
exercises.explanation: Two bare infinitives share one modal: wollen opens, anprobieren and spazieren ride inside — each keeps its full dictionary form in the bracket.

summary.outcome: Dissect any regular infinitive into its stem and rebuild all six persons.

use_example.english: We want to try things on and go for a stroll.

summary.takeaway: Stem + six tiles (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en) is the entire regular verb system — no tables needed.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Thou -st Circuit — drill the Shakespearean ending across five verbs until it is muscle memory.

twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir wollen anprobieren und spazieren" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Stem Hunters without relying on short-term echo.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

bringen.etymology_derivation: Shared ancient Germanic mixed verb (bring/brought ↔ bringen/gebracht).

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

setzen.context_phrase: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
setzen.context_translation: I sit down on the chair.
setzen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, a causative of sit; the page documents cognate English set. The t of set reappears as z (ts) in setzen, the same sibilant shift as two and zwei. [wiktionary]

sitzen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
sitzen.context_translation: We are sitting in the café.

halten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *haldaną — English hold is the documented cognate; German hardened d to t (the stop shift). Strong verb, class 7: hielt, gehalten. [wiktionary]

stehen.context_phrase: Ich stehe am Fenster und sehe hinaus.
stehen.context_translation: I stand at the window and look out.
stehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stāną; the page documents cognate English stand, the same stand-verb family (English stood, German stand). [wiktionary]

zeigen.context_phrase: Kannst du mir den Weg zeigen?
zeigen.context_translation: Can you show me the way?
zeigen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zeigōn, an intensive of zīhan; the page traces it to PIE *deyḱ- and notes that the root also gave Zeichen and English teach. The t of teach corresponds to the z of zeigen. [wiktionary]

küssen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kussijan — English kiss is the documented cognate; a doubled expressive kk that both languages kept. [wiktionary]

anprobieren.context_translation: I would like to try on the jacket.
anprobieren.etymology_derivation: an- + probieren (to try), from Latin probare - a verb of the French-derived -ieren family; as a separable verb it keeps ge- inside: anprobiert. [wiktionary]

spazieren.english_cognate: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.english_meaning: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian spaziare, from Latin spatiari, to stroll — an -ieren verb; English space is from the same Latin spatium. [wiktionary]
